concepts.name: Macronutrient types and roles
concepts.summary: Name carbohydrates, proteins and fats and state the main job of each in the body.

concepts.name: Calories as energy units
concepts.summary: Explain that calories measure the energy food provides and that bodies need a steady supply to function.

concepts.name: Water and hydration
concepts.summary: Explain why the body needs water and recognise signs of poor hydration such as thirst and dark urine.

concepts.name: Food groups
concepts.summary: List the main food groups and give examples of foods in each.

concepts.name: Why micronutrients are needed
concepts.summary: Recognise that vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts for body processes and that a varied diet supplies them.

concepts.name: Dietary fibre
concepts.summary: Describe what fibre is, which foods contain it and why it supports digestion.

misconceptions.text: All fats are bad for you and should be avoided completely.
Calories are something harmful in food rather than a measure of energy.
Only thirst tells you that you need water, and only plain water counts toward hydration.

concepts.name: Reading nutrition labels
concepts.summary: Find serving size, calories and nutrient amounts on a label and compute totals for the portion actually eaten.

concepts.name: Energy balance equation
concepts.summary: Explain how intake versus expenditure leads to weight gain, loss or maintenance.

concepts.name: Types of carbohydrate
concepts.summary: Distinguish sugars, starches and fibre and choose foods accordingly in everyday meals.

concepts.name: Fat types and sources
concepts.summary: Classify foods by main fat type and prefer unsaturated sources over saturated and trans fats.

concepts.name: Protein sources and quality
concepts.summary: Describe essential amino acids and identify animal and plant protein sources.

concepts.name: Matching key nutrients to foods
aliases: iron calcium vitamin C vitamin D sources
concepts.summary: Match specific nutrients such as iron, calcium, vitamin C and vitamin D to their main food sources and functions.

concepts.name: Balanced plate building
concepts.summary: Assemble a meal with appropriate proportions of vegetables, protein, starch and fat.

misconceptions.text: A product labelled low fat is automatically healthy or low in calories.
The nutrition panel values describe the whole package rather than one serving.
All carbohydrates are equally unhealthy and should be cut out.

concepts.name: Estimating energy needs
concepts.summary: Estimate basal metabolic rate and total daily energy expenditure from body size, age and activity level.

concepts.name: Setting macronutrient targets
concepts.summary: Set protein, carbohydrate and fat ranges suited to a person's goal and activity.

concepts.name: Glycaemic response and carbohydrate quality
concepts.summary: Analyse how food composition, fibre and processing affect blood glucose response.

concepts.name: Meal planning for goals
concepts.summary: Build a multi-day meal plan that meets energy and nutrient targets within budget and preferences.

concepts.name: Dietary pattern comparison
concepts.summary: Compare dietary patterns by foods emphasised, nutrient strengths and likely gaps.

concepts.name: Nutrient gaps and deficiencies
concepts.summary: Identify nutrients at risk in particular diets or life stages and the foods that address them.

concepts.name: Hydration and electrolytes
concepts.summary: Apply fluid and electrolyte guidance to exercise, heat and illness situations.

misconceptions.text: Calorie needs calculated from a formula are exact and never need adjusting.
Low glycaemic index foods are always healthy and high glycaemic index foods always unhealthy.
A vegetarian or vegan diet is inherently deficient or inherently complete without planning.

concepts.name: Appraising nutrition evidence
concepts.summary: Judge nutrition studies by design, confounding, outcomes measured and funding.

concepts.name: Evaluating popular diet claims
concepts.summary: Assess diets such as low-carb, keto and intermittent fasting for mechanism, evidence and sustainability.

concepts.name: Adaptive thermogenesis and weight regulation
concepts.summary: Analyse how metabolism, appetite hormones and activity adapt to weight change and shape plateaus.

concepts.name: Nutrient timing and sports fuelling
concepts.summary: Evaluate fuelling, protein and recovery strategies for different training demands.

concepts.name: Supplement efficacy and safety
concepts.summary: Weigh evidence, dose, interactions and regulation to decide when a supplement is justified.

concepts.name: Ultra-processed food and satiety
concepts.summary: Analyse how processing, energy density and palatability influence intake and health outcomes.

concepts.name: Nutrition for health conditions
concepts.summary: Evaluate dietary adjustments for conditions such as hypertension, type 2 diabetes and high cholesterol.

misconceptions.text: Any weight loss plateau means the person is miscounting or lacking willpower, not that physiology adapted.
Supplements are harmless because they are natural and can fill any dietary gap.
A single observational study showing an association proves a food causes or prevents disease.

concepts.name: Synthesising conflicting nutrition evidence
concepts.summary: Reconcile discordant trials, cohorts and meta-analyses into calibrated, hedged conclusions.

concepts.name: Behaviour change in dietary practice
concepts.summary: Create strategies that sustain dietary change using adherence, environment and motivation principles.

concepts.name: Individualised nutrition design
concepts.summary: Design a complete plan integrating physiology, medical history, preferences, culture and constraints.

concepts.name: Critiquing dietary guidelines
concepts.summary: Evaluate how guidelines are built, their evidence limits, and industry or policy influences.

concepts.name: Nutrigenomics and microbiome limits
concepts.summary: Judge the current strength and practical value of genetic and microbiome based dietary advice.

concepts.name: Food systems and sustainability tradeoffs
concepts.summary: Develop dietary recommendations that balance nutrient adequacy, environmental impact, cost and access.

misconceptions.text: Personalised nutrition based on DNA or microbiome tests reliably predicts the best diet for an individual.
Official dietary guidelines are purely objective summaries of settled science.
The diet that performs best in trials on average is the best choice for every client.
